值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入了解台灣高鐵從1974年構想提出到2007年正式通車，歷經33年波折與幾度瀕臨破產的起伏歷史。
  • 揭開高鐵路線與車站選址背後的政商博弈，理解當年政府如何透過路線妥協以遏止土地投機炒作。
  • 解析這項號稱全球最大BOT案的競標內幕，看民間財團如何以「政府零出資」的承諾奪標卻隨即陷入千億融資困境。

摘要

從一日生活圈到瀕臨破產的逆境之路

作者指出，2007年1月5日台灣高鐵正式通車，板橋至左營僅需90分鐘，徹底改寫了台灣西部的交通版圖，不僅讓一日生活圈成真，更使曾經黃金一時的北高航線走入歷史。到了2023年，高鐵年載客量突破8,000萬人次，但這項大眾習以為常的交通工具，在通車初期卻曾遭消保團體抵制並被民代痛批為「廢鐵」，營運僅兩年半就虧損三分之二資本額。這項歷時33年才落成的建設，經歷過預算全刪、列車轉向以及財務危機等重重考驗。

超級鐵路構想與防炒地的設站妥協

高鐵的起點可追溯至1970年代十大建設時期，台鐵早在1974年便提出「超級鐵路」研究，卻因國道興建資金不足而擱置。直到1980年代西部走廊交通嚴重癱瘓，行政院於1987年重啟可行性研究，最終在1990年拍板採用技術成熟的鋼輪鋼軌系統。原先規劃沿西部內陸興建，卻引發各方搶購周邊土地、地價飆漲的爭議；時任行政院長郝柏村為抑制炒地皮，一度將路線大幅移往海線，隨後因地方反彈，最終妥協於內陸與海線之間，將青埔、六家、烏日、太保、沙崙等站設於人煙稀少的農地上。

立院刪除預算催生全球最大BOT案

高鐵興建預算隨後膨脹至4,200億元以上，龐大的支出引發社會激烈爭論。1993年，立法院在王建煊等立委主導下，以極小差距全數刪除94億元的籌備預算，堅持政府不出一毛錢、應由民間全額出資。這項政治決策迫使交通部火速推動制定獎參條例，催生了以BOT模式（興建、營運、移轉）推動高鐵。然而，這項規模超越英法海底隧道的全球最大BOT案，隨即引發民間財團是否有能力負擔、銀行是否願意承貸的巨大問號。

五大家族零出資承諾與融資難關

1996年交通部公告招標後，形成了大陸工程殷琪結盟富邦、長榮等企業的「五大家族」台灣高鐵聯盟，與劉泰英領軍的中華高鐵聯盟展開對決。在這場看誰向政府要最少錢的競賽中，中華高鐵要求政府挹注近1,500億元，而台灣高鐵聯盟則開出政府零出資並於營運後回饋10%稅前盈餘的誘人條件，成功奪得最優議約權。然而，號稱完全由民間買單的高鐵案，在得標後隨即面臨近2,800億元龐大聯貸資金沒有銀行敢承接的嚴峻現實。

================================================

On the morning of January 5, 2007, a calm and pleasant day, as the clock struck 7:00, orange and white trains departed simultaneously from Banqiao and Zuoying stations. Racing across the western plains at top speeds of 300 km/ h, both arrived at their destinations at 8:30. From that day on, the journey between Banqiao and Zuoying took only 90 minutes, shaving two and a half hours off the travel time between the north and the south. On this day, Taiwan officially became one of the few countries in Asia to operate a high-speed railway. This line fundamentally rewrote the transportation landscape of western Taiwan, making a " one-day living circle"—a morning meeting in Taipei followed by dinner in. Kaohsiung—a reality. The Taipei-Kaohsiung flights, once a " golden route," officially ceased operations and became history after the final flight on August 31, 2012. By 2023 , the High Speed Rail carried 82.07 million passengers annually, crossing the 80 million mark for the first time. During this year’s Mid-Autumn Festival, the HSR even packed in 348,000 passengers in a single day, setting a new record since its inception. It is hard to imagine that this company was on the verge of bankruptcy 11 years ago. Even harder to imagine is that, before opening, consumer advocacy groups called for a boycott, and lawmakers blasted the HSR, claiming it performed worse than the conventional rail and should be. renamed "junk rail." This commuting tool you’ve grown accustomed to actually took a full 33 years to become a reality, counting from the first study conducted in 1974. Along the way, the project faced suspensions, budgets were slashed by the Legislative Yuan, and while European trains were originally planned , a fatal accident and a major earthquake led to Japanese trains being chosen instead. Just two and a half years after opening, accumulated losses had eaten up two-thirds of its capital. In the end, despite the winning bidder promising the government wouldn't need to pay a cent, the government has now become the HSR's largest shareholder. Next January marks the 20th anniversary. of the HSR. Today, we will take you back to look at how this project, once billed as the world's largest BOT case, was built and how it survived the brink of bankruptcy. Hi, this is Xiao Niu. Welcome to "Xiao Niu Talks Finance and Economics." To tell the story of the HSR , let's take a time machine back to the Ten Major Construction Projects of the 1970s. In that era, Taiwan's economy was taking off, with people and goods all crowding into the western corridor. The government finally completed the Sun Yat-sen Freeway—what is now National Highway No. 1—and electrified the western trunk railway line, successfully opening up the two main transportation arteries of the west. But at the same. time, next door in Japan, the Shinkansen had already been running for 10 years, making the conventional railway authorities quite envious. According to the Railway Bureau of the Ministry of Transportation and Communications, the concept of building a new high-speed railway in Taiwan can be traced back to a 1974 study by the Taiwan Railways Administration, with a very era-specific title: "A Study on the Development and Construction of a Super Railway." However, at that time, the freeway had just been completed, and the government didn't have enough spare funds to build this "super railway," so the plan was quickly shelved; but it wasn't long before the western corridor became a problem. It was jammed again. That was the era of Taiwan's economic takeoff. About 90%of the entire population lived. along the line from Taipei to Kaohsiung . Driving back to Kaohsiung during the holidays meant being stuck in traffic for eight or nine hours! Train tickets were sold out, and buses and unlicensed shuttles were completely packed. Consequently, in 1987, the then-Premier Yu Kuo-hwa instructed the Ministry of Transportation and Communications to submit a feasibility study report for a new high-speed rail. By 1990, the report was released. It compared several different modes, including increasing the speed of existing Taiwan Railways trains, building a brand-new high-speed railway, or even using magnetic levitation trains, which were very popular at the time. The final conclusion was that building a brand-new high-speed rail using the.

technologically mature steel-wheel and steel-rail system was the most economically efficient choice. In July of that same year, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications established the High-Speed Rail Engineering Preparatory Office. Initially, the government's plan was to build the high-speed rail along the western interior. However, local representatives and conglomerates with access to inside information immediately moved in to purchase land around these proposed station sites. Even before the locations of these stations were finalized, local land prices had already skyrocketed! Therefore, in 1991, then-Premier Hau Pei-tsun overturned the Ministry of Transportation's original route plan and moved the high-speed rail line and its stations to the coastal. areas. The reasoning at the time was, first, to disperse the urban population and spur the development of new towns; second, land was cheaper, avoiding controversy over mass expropriation of private homes; and the most crucial third reason was to curb land speculation—by moving stations to remote areas, he wanted to see how they would continue to drive up prices. However, as soon as the coastal route was announced , local governments immediately pushed back, arguing that it would lead to low usage efficiency for the high-speed rail stations. So, in October 1991, Hau Pei-tsun decided to adopt a compromise, charting a new route between the coastal and original inland lines, with seven stations from north to south: Taipei,. Taoyuan Qingpu, Hsinchu Liujia, Taichung Wuri, Chiayi Taibao, Tainan Shalun, and Kaohsiung Zuoying. Many of these stations were located on undeveloped farmland, and even the then-Director of the High Speed Rail Preparatory Office, Mao Chih-kuo, admitted that from a transport functional perspective, these stations were arguably redundant. As for the overall construction budget, it ballooned steadily, reaching over 420 billion NT dollars. Faced with such an expensive high-speed rail, was it really necessary to spend this money? Was it so urgent that it had to be built right then? Sure enough, these questions immediately exploded in the Legislative Yuan. In 1993, the Executive Yuan proposed a 9.4 billion NT dollar. high-speed rail budget, which was completely deleted after three votes in the Legislative Yuan by a slim margin, led by legislator Wang Chien-shien, a former Minister of Finance. They emphasized that they did not oppose building the high-speed rail, but because of the heavy national fiscal burden and frequent corruption in public sector projects, they argued that the rail should be funded by the private sector, with the government contributing not a single cent. Is it really possible to have the private sector pay for this incredibly expensive high-speed rail? If the government doesn't pay, letting private consortia fund the rail, the question is , would these groups really shell out. money for such an unprofitable project? The Ministry of Transportation and Communications worked around the clock to push through the "Statute for Encouraging Private Participation in Transportation Infrastructure Projects, " which was enacted in 1994. This is the well-known BOT model, or Build-Operate-Transfer, where the private sector builds and operates before transferring it back. It means the private sector provides the funds to build and operate for a period to recoup their investment, and after the term expires, the entire railway is transferred to the government. However, the scale of Taiwan's high-speed rail BOT was larger than the world's most expensive BOT project at the time, the Channel Tunnel between the UK and France . This created a problem: if the government truly paid nothing, could any. single consortium afford such a massive sum? Would banks really be willing to lend money to these consortia to build a high-speed rail that might not even be profitable? But the high-speed rail still held its own appeal, after all. After the Ministry of Transportation and Communications announced the tender in 1996, two groups ultimately stepped forward to compete. On one side is the Taiwan High Speed Rail Consortium, led by Continental Engineering's Nita Ing, who brought in Evergreen, Fubon, Pacific Electric Wire&Cable, and TECO; the media dubbed them the "Five Great Families." On the other side is the Chung Hwa High Speed Rail Consortium, headed by China Development Industrial Bank Chairman and KMT treasurer Liu Tai-ying. On one side are the second generation of business leaders; on the other are veterans holding the vast resources of party-owned enterprises. The rules of.

the game were simple: it was a contest to see who would ask the government for the least amount of money. On September 25, 1997, the evaluation committee opened the bidding documents, and the winner was revealed once and for all. Chung Hwa HSR's condition was for the government to invest another 149.5 billion NTD, but the Taiwan HSR Consortium’s proposal not only required zero government funding but also promised that after operations began, they would contribute 10%of their pre-tax operating profits back to the government annually. For the government , it was clear even with eyes closed which side’s offer was better! The Taiwan HSR Consortium relied on this absolute advantage of zero government funding to win the priority negotiation. rights. They officially signed the contract with the Ministry of Transportation and Communications. While it was claimed there would be zero government funding, banks were terrified to lend for a project of this hundred-billion-dollar scale. By 1999, nearly 280 billion NTD in financing remained unsecured, and rumors of contract termination began to spread. This led their original competitor, Liu Tai-ying, to publicly remark that if he had to clean up the mess, he could, but he had zero interest in high-speed rail because it was simply impossible to make money. In the end, the government had to step in to resolve the crisis. A tripartite agreement was signed between the Ministry of Transportation and Communications, the HSR company, and the banking syndicate, with the government guaranteeing the loans; if the HSR. project failed, the government would have to step in and take over. Just like that, in February 2000, the syndicated loan of over 300 billion NTD was finally secured, and by March, the civil construction of the high-speed rail began in full. However, the timing was quite delicate; just two months after construction started, Taiwan saw its first peaceful transfer of power. The plan was set by the KMT government, and the contract was signed by the KMT government, but the party left to see it through to completion was the DPP, under the leadership of Chen Shui-bian. Money. With the problem temporarily settled, the next question was: whose trains should they buy? As mentioned earlier, the Taiwan HSR Consortium’s partners during the bidding process were. the European High Speed Rail Consortium —namely Germany's Siemens and France's Alstom—while the rival Chung Hwa HSR system was partnered with Japan's Shinkansen system. The Taiwan High Speed Rail consortium's initial proposal was quite bold: using a German ICE power head to pull French TGV double-decker carriages. Because of this, the high-speed rail's technical specifications were based on European systems from the start, and most of the consultants hired were European or American engineers. Logically speaking, Taiwan should be running European trains today, but nobody expected a single accident to change everything. On June 3 , 1998, shortly before 11:00 AM, a German ICE train was passing through the small northern German town of Eschede at. 200 kilometers per hour. Suddenly, a wheel tire fractured due to metal fatigue. The train derailed and struck a nearby road bridge, causing the entire bridge to collapse onto the carriages, killing 101 people. This remains the most severe accident in high-speed rail history. Footage of this accident reached Taiwan, and everyone was shocked , as the European-spec trains intended for Taiwan's high-speed rail were to use the German ICE power heads. The second unexpected event was the massive earthquake that struck in the early morning of September 21, 1999, claiming over 2,400 lives. Overnight, the Taiwanese people realized something: for a train running at 300 kilometers per hour in a seismic zone, the first. question isn't how fast it goes, but whether it can stop when an earthquake hits. At this point, the shrewd Japanese businessmen naturally wouldn't miss this perfect opportunity for a comeback, as their Shinkansen's greatest strength is automatically triggering emergency brakes before destructive seismic waves arrive. In November of that same year, they came to Taiwan High Speed Rail to give a technical presentation, and things changed right there. >> Things had changed. >> The Japanese side's overall bid was 35 billion NTD cheaper than the European-spec trains, while also offering low-interest loans. The Japanese also brought in newer train models, and sure enough, they.

successfully hooked the "big fish" that was Taiwan High Speed Rail. On December 28, 1999, Taiwan High Speed Rail held an extraordinary board meeting and announced that the major 95 billion NTD electrical and mechanical contract would be awarded to the Japan-led Taiwan Shinkansen Consortium. The Europeans were furious and immediately took the case to international arbitration. The lawsuit lasted until 2004, and in the end, the high-speed rail operator had to pay 89 million USD in damages and interest. There were several conspiracy theories at the time. Some questioned whether the Taiwan High Speed Rail consortium had used a low-price bid to lock in European specs, only to realize after winning that the funding gap was too large, leading them to deliberately make things difficult for the European side before finally turning to the. cheaper Japanese trains. There were also rumors that the switch in trains was because President Lee Teng-hui, before stepping down, wanted to strengthen Taiwan-Japan relations by gifting this nearly 100-billion-dollar procurement deal to Japan as a parting gift. However , Taiwan High Speed Rail never confirmed these rumors, denying any political considerations. By December 2000, Taiwan High Speed Rail officially signed a contract with the Japanese side. This marked the first time Japanese Shinkansen technology was exported overseas; Japan used their 700 Series as a template to custom-build the 700T for Taiwan. At this point, problems followed . Civil engineering work on the high-speed rail had already been underway for nine months, with bridges and tunnels designed to European. specifications. The consultants in the company were still that same group of European and American experts. Now, they had to install a full Japanese electrical and mechanical system onto foundations laid by Europeans—the so-called "Euro-Japan" blend. "Hybrid system"—those four words started right here. At this point in the story, I ask everyone to please click subscribe. Clicking subscribe is easy for you, and it won't affect your YouTube homepage algorithm at all. But for us, the subscription count is the most tangible encouragement, and it helps us get noticed by potential sponsors. One subscriber, one person happy; 300,000 subscribers, 300,000 people happy. Together. In March 2000, high-speed rail construction officially began, with 330. kilometers of worksites from north to south springing into action almost simultaneously. The entire high-speed rail line is 345 kilometers long, with over 300 kilometers consisting of either bridges or tunnels. The bridge section alone accounts for about 250 kilometers , meaning the entire railway is basically suspended in mid-air. At the time, the Taiwan High Speed Rail Corporation divided the entire civil engineering project into 12 tenders, with teams composed of 12 domestic and international construction firms working separately. Major players from Japan and Germany all came—truly worthy of being the largest BOT project in the world. But the project had just begun, and trouble arrived. The first hurdle was the aftermath of the 921 earthquake. After the quake, the government revised the seismic design standards for public works, which meant designs that were already halfway finished had to be redone. The High Speed Rail Corporation estimated that costs would skyrocket by 30 to 40 percent. However, after a later review, it was determined that the original standards were sufficient, and they were changed back in September 2000. This back-and-forth wasted about five months. The second hurdle occurred underground. The Hukou Tunnel in Hsinchu collapsed twice, and even the High Speed Rail Corporation couldn't name the exact cause. Down south, the soil was wet and soft, posing a risk whenever an earthquake occurred. To visualize this, each bridge pier requires a foundation pile two meters in diameter and about 60 meters deep, which is like burying a 20. -story building's worth of column into the ground. The third hurdle was the 2003 SARS outbreak. The construction sites relied heavily on foreign migrant workers; when the epidemic hit, many chose to return home. The team in the Taichung area suddenly lost about 20%of its workforce, forcing them to take temperatures twice a day and work overtime to get back on schedule. So the question is, why did a project that almost saw its contract terminated before construction even began manage to be built successfully and open to traffic after breaking ground in March 2000? Below, we have summarized four answers. The first answer is that, according to the contract, the government was responsible for land.

acquisition for tracks and stations, as well as the underground sections in Taipei. The High Speed Rail Corporation didn't have to buy land parcel by parcel and could focus on building its 330 kilometers. The second answer lies in the bridges. About two-thirds of the high-speed rail is elevated, using full-span precast construction. The bridge spans were not poured section by section on-site, but rather precast at a facility as entire 800-ton box girders, then moved forward by special machinery —just like a factory assembly line. One team in the central region installed nearly 700 of these pieces. From Baguashan in Changhua to Zuoying in Kaohsiung, this formed a continuous 157. -kilometer elevated bridge. When completed in 2004, it was the world's longest bridge, only later surpassed by China's Jin-Hu High-Speed Railway. The third answer is in the contract: all 12 civil engineering contracts were design-build projects. These were turnkey contracts, and there were penalties for delays. As a result, construction began in March 2000 and the civil engineering was declared finished in January 2005. That is less than five years in total, with some sections even completed ahead of schedule. The final, fourth answer is more controversial: full government backing. When then-President Chen Shui-bian inspected the Yanchao depot, he stated, "The high-speed rail must succeed, it cannot fail; the government will remove any. obstacles for it." So, during the construction period, the high-speed rail held several rounds of capital increases . When private shareholders were reluctant to add more, the ones who finally stepped in were state-run enterprises like Taiwan Sugar, the National Development Fund, and public banks that purchased 17.3 billion NTD in preferred shares all at once. In 2005, the High Speed Rail announced a one-year delay in operations due to mechanical and electrical engineering setbacks; this single year of delay burned through an extra 20 billion NTD, with the funding gap filled once again by the 4.5 billion from the Aviation Development Foundation and 3 billion from the China Aviation Development Foundation. Then-Premier Frank Hsieh later stated that he had requested the Aviation Development Foundation and other such entities to assist in increasing the High Speed Rail’s capital, which drew sharp criticism from the opposition KMT. for blurring the lines between public and private interests. The Executive Yuan argued that public investment had not exceeded the limit and did not violate the premise of zero government funding, but KMT legislators questioned whether this was a complete betrayal of the commitments made when the Taiwan High Speed Rail Corporation first won the bid. The Control Yuan later issued a corrective proposal, arguing that the investment from public treasuries invited controversy and that the government's guarantee risks were rising . Combined with the fact that in the 2000 presidential election, the company had publicly supported Chen Shui-bian, all major and minor controversies surrounding the High Speed Rail took on a layer of blue-green political maneuvering. So, was the High Speed Rail built quickly or not? From the start of construction in March 2000 to the. official launch, it took six years and ten months; the civil engineering portion was completed in less than five years, outpacing the Sun Yat-sen Freeway , the Formosa Freeway, and the Taipei Metro. THSRC CEO Ou Chin-der, who had a background as a government official under the KMT, later said that despite facing a severe labor shortage during the SARS outbreak in 2003, the High Speed Rail launched only one year behind schedule, which is remarkable by any global standard. However, in reality, completing the civil engineering was only the first half; what really caused the delay in opening was the mechanical and electrical system—the very thing mentioned earlier. Is the High Speed Rail system truly a hybrid of European and Japanese technology? Let’s look at. the "yes" side: The Japanese side listed a total of 26 areas where it differed from the Shinkansen, the most famous of which is bidirectional signaling. For 40 years, the Japanese Shinkansen has run in only one direction per track, but Taiwan's High Speed Rail followed the European approach, requiring both directions to run on the same track so that if one side has trouble, trains can pass through the other side. This single requirement gave the Japanese mechanical and electrical personnel a massive headache, causing progress to fall behind by 20 percent at one point. Ultimately, this is a difference between two distinct railway cultures. European high-speed rail prioritizes automation and flexibility, while the Shinkansen emphasizes human discipline and stability. The High Speed Rail Corporation called this combination the.

"Best Mix," meaning to take the strengths of each, but JR Central, which provided the technical resources, did not buy into it. JR Central consultant Hiroshi Tanaka warned that system integration would be a significant challenge. According to a report by Next Magazine at the time, JR Central issued an ultimatum in September 2004, stating that if these discrepancies were not resolved, they could no longer support the Taiwan High Speed Rail. After that, THSRC Chairman Nita Ing flew to Japan time and again to communicate. The cover of the weekly magazine at the time directly featured the headline " Dangerous High-Speed Rail," and a phrase circulated online: "Such a dangerous high-speed rail, would you dare to ride it?" Looking at the other side, in an interview with CommonWealth Magazine, Ing spoke very directly, stating that. there was no such thing as a " European-Japanese hybrid" system. Her argument was that the core electrical and mechanical systems of the high-speed rail were entirely Japanese Shinkansen, and the 26 points of difference were merely additional requirements built upon the Shinkansen foundation. THSRC executives also explained that most of these differences were intended to enhance safety, using technology to reduce human error. So, who was actually right? Engineer Masashi Oguchi, who participated in the high-speed rail project from the Japanese side, wrote a retrospective piece many years later. He said that the outside claim— "Japanese trains, French systems"—was incorrect. The high-speed rail was indeed built on Shinkansen technology. However, he also noted that after the Japanese side won. the bid, there were still many European and American technical personnel within the company, and both sides argued for a long time, from technical aspects to concepts. The final result was the Shinkansen combined with quite a few European-style devices and functions. In other words, the signaling system was Japanese, the bridges and tunnels were of European specifications, the trains were operated by French and German drivers, and the operations control center communicated in English. How could this unprecedented combination be proven safe? At that time, the high-speed rail had to pass three major hurdles. The first was to resolve each of the 26 discrepancies one by one. The second was to hire independent third-party international agencies for inspection; they brought in the British. Lloyd's Register for independent verification and validation, while seeking German agencies for the certification of signaling components. The Japanese were very unaccustomed to this at first, because the Shinkansen had been running for 40 years without ever being inspected by outsiders like this. The third hurdle was approval from the Taiwan government, specifically the Ministry of Transportation and Communications, and they almost didn't make it past this stage. In January 2005 , test runs began between Tainan and Kaohsiung. On October 30 of that same year, the train reached a speed of 315 km/h, setting a new record for the fastest rail speed in Taiwan. However, progress on the electrical and mechanical systems for other sections lagged behind, and the test runs were delayed until the end of 2006. Unexpectedly, a derailment occurred. during a test run in Chiayi. To prove the high-speed rail system was perfectly safe, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications decided to adopt the most stringent testing conditions: two weeks of continuous, intensive trial runs— simulating departures every four minutes , single-track bidirectional operations , train passing, and emergency stops— plus a month of accident-free operation . If even one accident occurred, the count would reset to zero. Then-Premier Su Tseng-chang also stated in the Legislative Yuan that safety was the only principle for opening the line, declaring that if the inspection was not passed, he would not attend the opening ceremony. Meanwhile, the Legislative Yuan was in an uproar. On December 24, 2006, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications announced that the. high-speed rail met the standards for operation. Opposition lawmakers immediately launched a verbal barrage, arguing that Su Tseng-chang was gambling with the lives of citizens to boost his prospects for the 2008 presidential election. They demanded that Su should stake his own political future on the safety of the passengers. External opinions were also divided. NTU Professor Chang Hsueh-kung believed that the international certification body responsible for verification held a high level of credibility. Their verification results should be respected. However, the Consumers 'Foundation criticized the Ministry of Transportation and Communications for dismissing the items that needed improvement before the opening with a single phrase: "all have been addressed." They immediately initiated a nationwide campaign to " refuse the high-speed rail," and KMT.

lawmakers also pledged their cooperation . Amidst the booming criticism and widespread skepticism, on January 5, 2007, this high-speed railway that cuts across the north and south, which everyone had waited over 30 years for, finally...On the day the high-speed rail opened, according to later accounts from then-Deputy Minister of Transportation Ho Nuan-hsuan, there were no ceremonies and no firecrackers. A foreign driver sat in the cockpit because the local drivers wouldn't be ready to officially take over until May. At the moment of the maiden voyage, everyone was on edge . After all, the immense public pressure meant they didn't even dare to hold a ribbon-cutting ceremony or beat drums. They could only silently bid farewell to. the driver and passengers of the first train. Just like that, this major infrastructure project, built at a cost of hundreds of billions, began its journey quietly without many blessings, step by step changing the lifestyle and transportation landscape of western Taiwan. However, after the opening, small and large incidents continued. Trains reversing into stations, ticket machines spitting out piles of coins, delays, and smoke in the carriages— these situations led KMT lawmakers to directly mock the high-speed rail as " scrap metal," demanding that the Taiwan High Speed Rail Corporation immediately cease operations. But the tides turned quickly. On April 1st, former Kuomintang Chairman Ma Ying-jeou, who had previously refused to ride the. High-Speed Rail, decided to take it to Tainan for an event. After getting off, he praised the ride as smooth and comfortable, rivaling Japan's Shinkansen and France's TGV. From that day on, no one dared to call the High-Speed Rail " scrap metal" or "junk" anymore. But is this system really safe? Its toughest test came on March 4, 2010, at 8:18 AM, when a magnitude 6.4 earthquake struck Jiaxian, Kaohsiung. At the time, six high-speed trains were operating near the epicenter, and all of them immediately initiated emergency braking . Although one of the northbound trains derailed in Tainan, all 300-plus passengers on board were evacuated. safely. Nearly seven years after opening , the High-Speed Rail Bureau’s report stated: over 250 million passengers served, zero accidents resulting in passenger casualties, and a punctuality rate as high as 99.4%. However, while the High-Speed Rail passed the safety test, it nearly collapsed on its balance sheet. Initial estimates projected 180,000 to 230,000 passengers per day, but the first year averaged just over 40,000. With heavy interest on hundreds of billions in loans and a concession period of only 35 years, depreciation costs left the Taiwan High Speed Rail Corporation gasping for air. By 2009, the rail's cumulative losses had wiped. out two-thirds of its capital, forcing Chairman Nita Ing to resign in sorrow and leave his post. Why did the financial situation of the High-Speed Rail deteriorate so sharply? It actually had something to do with Nita Ing. At the time, he was not only the High-Speed Rail Chairman, but the Continental Engineering Corporation behind him had also undertaken the rail's civil construction works. Within the same group, his left hand was a major investor, while his right hand was the contractor receiving construction fees. Construction payments flowed out of the High-Speed Rail company, and the recipient was also a major shareholder of the High-Speed Rail. Investors naturally want project costs to be as low as possible, but those undertaking the civil engineering want the project fees to be as high as possible. As a. result, these two conflicting roles were tied to the same group associated with Nita Ing. Should they help the company save money, or help the company make money? The blurring of this line became a ticking time bomb for the High-Speed Rail's financial ruin. By 2014, the High-Speed Rail Corporation still had over 46 billion in cumulative losses on its books, along with 360 billion in accumulated debt. If financial reforms weren't implemented quickly, the High-Speed Rail would face bankruptcy as early as March of the following year. With its financial situation in dire straits, the High Speed Rail was forced to launch a financial restructuring plan . The first step was a 60%capital reduction, followed by a government-led.

capital injection of 30 billion NTD, and finally, extending the franchise period to 70 years to amortize costs. Public sector shareholding rose to around 64%, turning the HSR into a state-run private enterprise. When the Taiwan High Speed Rail Corporation won the bid in 1997, it was promised that the government wouldn't need to spend a dime. Yet, the government eventually became the HSR's largest shareholder, remaining so to this day. Looking back at the HSR's operational performance, in its first year, it carried an average of just over 40,000 passengers a day. By 2015, that reached over 220,000 daily, totaling 82.07 million for the year. By March of this year, cumulative ridership. surpassed 1 billion, with an on-time rate exceeding 99%. Since operations began, there has been no record of passenger casualties due to accidents, completely shattering the rumors of it being "scrap metal" back then. Regarding its financial status, in the second quarter of 2016, the HSR's single-quarter revenue reached 13.9 billion NTD, compared to 10 billion NTD ten years prior, marking a growth of... ...nearly 40%, while the gross profit margin climbed from 3%to 41%. It's not just more profitable than before; the bottom-line profit has also increased, and the heavy financial burden weighing on the HSR has been reduced by nearly half. The story of the HSR, from planning to operation over these nearly. 50 years, is actually a microcosm of the government's policy-making process. People often start by shouting a nice slogan, leaving the hardest problems for later. But when the issues finally explode, they realize it's far more serious than imagined, and the true cost of solving them is unfathomable. Although the government's promise of zero funding ultimately fell through, the "one-day living circle" created by the HSR did become a reality. This experience has led the government to re-evaluate its logic for using the BOT model for major public projects. It can no longer use low subsidies and zero funding as primary criteria for selection; instead, it must rigorously. assess overall operational performance, financing caps, and establish clear default clauses. For so-called BOT projects, the government cannot simply cast off its responsibilities; only then can major public works achieve sustainable development. Next time you hear a project claimed to cost the government nothing, or another labeled as scrap metal, perhaps we can all ask one more question, wait a little longer , and let time provide the answer. When was the first time you took the high-speed rail? Do you remember if you dared to ride it the year it opened? Feel free to leave a comment below and help make the story more complete. Lastly, just a reminder: high-speed rail tickets for the November 28th election day are already on sale, and many trains. are selling out fast. The HSR has added 22 trains, including ten late-night discounted services with 30%off reserved seats. Don't worry about getting home to vote; book your tickets online now and go cast your important ballot.

摘要

從防疫光環到民意轉折

摘要

從防疫光環到民意轉折

作者回顧了2020年台灣面對COVID-19初期的情境。當時台灣創下連續253天零本土確診紀錄，每日下午兩點的疫情記者會成為全民焦點，時任衛福部長兼指揮中心指揮官的陳時中聲勢如日中天，全民掀起「順時中」風潮。在2020年4月的假想民調中，陳時中甚至以49%的支持度大幅領先國民黨立委蔣萬安，展現問鼎首都市長寶座的強大實力。

病毒變異引發的政策風暴與中央地方角力

然而，隨著病毒不斷變異，防疫神話面臨考驗。2021年Alpha變種病毒引爆諾富特飯店與機師群聚感染，在野黨強烈抨擊指揮中心放寬機組員檢疫為「3+11」的決策。隨後疫情蔓延至萬華引發全國三級警戒，官員稱萬華為「破口」更引發地方民怨。自此，中央與台北市展開激烈政治攻防，中央下午兩點召開記者會，台北市長柯文哲則於三點召開記者會分庭抗禮，雙方更圍繞在疫苗採購、國產高端疫苗與BNT疫苗爭議上針鋒相對。

共存轉型陣痛與2022首都選戰起跑

邁入2022年春季，傳染力強大的Omicron變種病毒肆虐，迫使指揮中心逐步放棄清零，轉向以減災為目標的「與病毒共存」。在政策急轉彎的過程中，伴隨快篩試劑短缺、停課與隔離標準反覆調整，以及餐飲觀光業重創，累積的民怨轉化為執政黨的沈重包袱。陳時中從昔日的抗疫領袖，逐漸成為政策代罪羔羊。此時年底地方大選戰鼓響起，對藍營而言，台北市已連續八年由非藍營執政，是絕不能再輸的關鍵戰役。

國民黨於2022年5月正式徵召形象清新的立委蔣萬安參選。然而蔣萬安出線初期團隊步調緩慢、行程低調，被外界諷為「佛系選舉」與「躺平」，引發藍營基層焦慮。6月初公布的民調顯示，蔣萬安雖位居首位，但與因第一線防疫累積高聲量的副市長黃珊珊差距甚微，兩人落入誤差範圍；反觀陳時中則受本土疫情與防疫爭議衝擊滑落至第三名，首都市長爭奪戰正式進入緊繃的三腳督競逐。

segment of independent voters. As for Chen Shih-chung, he fell to third place . The day after her announcement, a TVBS poll showed Chiang Wan-an and Huang Shan-shan both at 26%, with Chen Shih-chung at 23%, narrowing the gap between Chiang and Huang from the original 10%to just 3%. Even more surprising is that among voters aged 30 to 39, nearly half support Huang Shan-shan. For the Blue camp, they are facing enemies on both sides; attacking.

Chen Shih-chung benefits Huang, but attacking Huang risks offending Ko's supporters, cutting off their retreat path. It’s a similar headache for the Green camp, as Chen, backed by the party , still lagged in the August polls. Three candidates. As each candidate announced their run for Taipei mayor, policy became a key point of contention , and the first battlefield was the traffic in Neihu. Previously, due to Ko Wen-je’s remark that "Neihu traffic is beyond saving," the gridlock during rush hour has become a major battlefield in every mayoral election. Chen Shih-chung proposed solutions as soon as he announced his run. These four solutions. for Neihu's traffic include building new highway ramps and digging a tunnel under the Keelung River using shallow excavation methods; however, Huang Shan-shan poured cold water on these ideas. She argued that the biggest bottleneck in Neihu is actually Songshan Airport. In the long run, moving the airport would allow for new connecting bridges. She also criticized the DPP for only discussing moving the airport during mayoral elections. Chen responded that throwing out such big issues during a campaign is more about political posturing than municipal development. Interestingly, four years later, incumbent Chiang Wan-an, seeking re-election, also proposed a vision to abolish the airport and build an AI park . In any case, this prime piece of land at Songshan Airport seems to spark. everyone's imagination in almost every election. Speaking of Chiang Wan-an, his bus policy also left him red-faced. After his suggestion of booking bus seats online was mocked as impractical, he proposed doing 20 squats in exchange for a free bus ride. Although he claimed he was just citing someone else's idea, this whimsical notion was immediately mocked by Ko Wen-je, who remarked that it was about the level he expected from him. Meanwhile, the Chen campaign, aiming to woo young and female voters, visited bars, danced hip-hop, and held pink parties. While some saw him as letting his guard down, others felt it. was too forced. It created a huge disconnect from the steady, commander-in-chief image Chen had previously cultivated. Of course, when creativity is poorly handled, it can backfire badly; the most classic example being Chen Shih-chung’s bidet toilet advertisement. Shortly after announcing his candidacy, Chen Shih-chung proposed a "public restroom upgrade" policy, aiming to install bidet seats in the 7,200 restrooms managed by the Taipei City Government, hoping to mirror Japan and effectively improve the service quality of Taipei’s public facilities. Although both the KMT and TPP camps criticized the policy for its low feasibility, the initial intent was good . However, the advertisement launched by his team to promote this policy featured. Chen imitating a viral meme, showing him peeking over a restroom partition and flashing a peace sign at an internet celebrity inside. It was likely intended to be funny, but it reminded many netizens of a scene from a Korean film, turning a comedic attempt into something creepy. Although Chen Shih-chung quickly issued a public apology and took the video down, commentators bluntly pointed out that this was a very clear policy blunder. Following that, it was time to dig up old grievances, as the main battlefield for the three candidates returned to the issue of vaccines. In mid-August, the KMT legislative caucus revealed that documents related to vaccine procurement. were sealed for 30 years. Chiang Wan-an immediately launched an attack, questioning how one could trust Chen to manage a city budget of over 100 billion NTD annually when things were so opaque . The Chen camp retorted that 30 years is the standard retention period for major procurement documents, meaning they must be kept for 30 years, not that they cannot be disclosed for 30 years. They accused Chiang Wan-an of knowing the truth, given that he himself is the convener of the Legislative Yuan's vaccine investigation committee. However , the most damaging blow came from an unexpected bombshell thrown from the sidelines. In mid-September, veteran media personality Chou Yu-kou used her talk show to expose the lesser-known past of the Chiang family, ranging from the mystery of Chiang Wan-an’s ancestry to his father Chiang Hsiao-yen’s. extramarital affair from over 20 years ago. Faced with these media attacks, the usually mild-mannered Chiang took a firm stance: "If you have the guts, come after me directly; don't drag other people into this." But what really caused the situation to spiral out of control was on September 22nd, when Chou Yu-kou and another media figure, Tsai Yu-chen, directly named former Miss China Chang Shu-chuan as the woman involved in the affair during their program. The next day, Chang went to the Taipei District Prosecutors Office to file a lawsuit, tearfully recounting how she had been bullied and slandered. Unexpectedly, Chou appeared on the scene claiming she wanted to apologize to Chang in person, only to end up in a shouting match with City Councilor Wang Hung-wei, who was accompanying Chang, with both sides calling each other cockroaches and rats. This scene was.

later seen as a turning point that affected the election, and in this instance, it was actually Chen Shih-chung who ended up taking the hit. It is widely believed that Chou Yu-kou and Chen Shih-chung have a good relationship, leading many politicians to immediately declare that "supporting Chen Shih-chung is supporting Chou Yu-kou." Huang Shan-shan also stepped forward to support Chiang Wan-an, asking them if they had any conscience at all. Heart and conscience. As for Chen Shih-chung, he came forward to soften the situation, suggesting that everyone is an independent individual responsible for their own words. Although everyone made their corresponding stances known, in this wave of smear tactics, the real beneficiary was Chiang Wan-an, which was immediately reflected in the poll numbers. According to a TVBS poll in. early October, Chiang Wan-an's support jumped to 40%, Huang Shan-shan's was 23 %, and Chen Shih-chung's was 22%. Regarding this case, the Taipei District Prosecutors Office also indicted Chou and Tsai. In the latest second-instance verdict, Chou Yu-kou was sentenced to nine months, and Tsai Yu-chen... Entering the final month of the election , all three sides began to play their trump cards. On October 1st, Chen Shih-chung established his campaign headquarters, with Pan-Green heavyweights like Tsai Ing-wen, Lai Ching-te, Su Tseng-chang, and Chen Chien-jen all in attendance. On the same day, the KMT mobilized Chu Li-lun, Ma Ying-jeou, and Hou Yu-ih to secure the base for Chiang. As for Huang Shan-shan's side, former New Power Party chairman Huang Kuo-chang, who had not. yet joined the Taiwan People's Party, declared: "If I were a Taipei citizen, I would definitely vote for Huang Shan-shan." As the Blue and Green camps returned to their ranks and the base began to mobilize, the response rate in polls significantly increased. Chen Shih-chung's poll numbers saw an uptick , shaking off his entanglement with Huang Shan-shan. According to the early November poll by Formosa Magazine, Chiang Wan-an stood at 34.3%, Chen Shih-chung at 27.7%, and Huang Shan-shan at 22.4%, widening the gap between the three and making Chiang Wan-an's advantage more obvious. Now everyone is asking the same question: will there be "strategic voting"? Sure enough, the master of strategic voting, Broadcasting Corporation of China chairman Jaw. Shaw-kong, immediately made a move: the KMT supporting the TPP's Kao Hung-an in Hsinchu in exchange for the TPP supporting Chiang Wan-an in Taipei. Huang Shan-shan bitterly criticized Jaw Shaw-kong for engaging in naked political bartering, but this rhetoric did not have much impact on her polling situation. As mentioned earlier, Huang Shan-shan's voter base does not necessarily come from the Blue camp; a large portion consists of light-green supporters, and combined with her personal appeal, centrist voters are willing to buy in. These highly autonomous supporters are not easily swayed like those of Wang Chien-shien or James Soong in the past, who were eventually victims of strategic voting. On October 5th, the only televised debate of the entire election campaign. took place. Before the debate, everyone expected Huang Shan-shan, who is relatively familiar with municipal affairs, to perform better, believing she might dominate the stage and overshadow Chiang Wan-an and Chen Shih-chung. Unexpectedly, on the day of the debate, Chiang Wan-an put on his glasses and displayed a confident and fluent demeanor, which was in stark contrast to his past "soft" reputation. This sharp contrast left everyone with the impression that he performed much better than expected. As for Chen Shih-chung, he focused on an emotional appeal. Faced with overwhelming criticism regarding pandemic prevention and vaccine procurement, he directly appealed to emotions in his closing statement. He said, "I wanted to protect. everyone in Taiwan, but I failed to do so. I'm sorry, and thank you all for your hard work." Scholars analyzed this as an attempt to seek understanding and empathy from the citizens. He wanted to convey that even if he didn't succeed, he had worked hard. However, the day after the debate, KMT councilor Hsu Chiao-hsin released photos she claimed were provided by the public, accusing Chen of allegedly hugging and holding hands with a married female deputy hospital superintendent, portraying him as a "groping hand." Chen's campaign headquarters refuted Hsu's narrative, stating that there was no sign of any groping or sexual harassment in the photos. Regardless, the damage to Chen. Shih-chung from these leaked photos was already done. Official polls showed Chiang Wan-an at 36%, Chen Shih-chung at 25%, and Huang Shan-shan at 24%, showing that the gap between Chiang and Chen had widened once again. Even more subtle was the age demographic in the polls. In the TVBS final poll, 56%of those aged 20 to 29 supported Huang Shan-shan. CommonWealth Magazine also found that in polls over the last two months, Chen Shih-chung never led in this age group. The support of young people remained firmly with Ko Wen-je and Huang Shan-shan, which became a major reason why "strategic voting" was difficult to achieve. Finally, on the eve of the election, it rained heavily in Taipei. Chiang called out in the rain for.

everyone to embrace Taipei and Taiwan. Chen Shih-chung teared up on stage, saying those were tears shed because the achievements of pandemic prevention were smeared during the campaign. Huang Shan-shan chose the plaza in front of City Hall, also in the pouring rain, urging citizens to defend new values and break away from old forces. In this three-way race that fought bitterly from the end of the pandemic, who would finally emerge victorious? On the voting day of November 26th, the voter turnout in Taipei was about 68%, which is not considered high compared to previous elections. Once the votes were tallied, Chiang’s lead grew steadily throughout the night. Around 7:00 PM, Chen Shih-chung was the first to concede, inviting his supporters to join him in. wishing Chiang Wan-an well and expressing hope that the smear campaigns against pandemic prevention efforts would end there. When Huang Shan-shan addressed the crowd for her concession speech, she gave Mayor Ko Wen-je an emotional hug, thanking him for his mentorship and encouragement. At 8:00 PM , Chiang walked onto the stage to cheers of "Mr. Mayor," stating that citizens had used their votes to let kindness triumph over malice. He thanked his opponents, Chen and Huang, for their efforts. His father, Chiang Hsiao-yen, who had remained unseen throughout the campaign, appeared on stage at the final moment to give his son a big hug. In the final count, Chiang secured 570,000 votes, a 42%share; Chen Shih-chung took 430,000 votes, about 32%; and Huang. Shan-shan received 340,000 votes, totaling 25%. At 43 years old, Chiang was elected mayor of Taipei, becoming the youngest directly elected mayor in the city’s history. However, Chiang’s vote share was the lowest for a KMT candidate elected in Taipei, and Chen failed to secure the traditional Pan-Green base, performing only slightly better than Yao Wen-chih in 2018. The key factor was Huang Shan-shan; although she received far fewer votes than Ko Wen-je did four years ago, she was not completely squeezed out, holding onto a quarter of the total vote. Why did Chen Shih-chung lose? I believe his greatest asset and his biggest burden were actually the same thing: his role in pandemic prevention. Supporters remember. the commander who stood on stage at 2:00 PM sharp for over 900 days, but for other voters, memories of Wanhua, the " 3 + 11" policy, and vaccine issues were resurfaced throughout the campaign. Fairly speaking, many decisions made during the pandemic by all camps were made under time pressure with incomplete information; merits and faults are hard to summarize, but an election is a single-choice question, not a performance review. Add to that the controversies surrounding the social media team and the fallout from the Hsu Chun-chi incident, and it became difficult for Chen to expand his support in the final stage. As for Huang Shan-shan, although she captured most of the independent voters and had the lowest "negativity rating" of the three. , the approval rating for the Ko administration remained low, failing to garner enough praise for municipal performance to expand her base. Her final vote count was 240,000 lower than when Ko was re-elected four years ago. And why did Chiang Wan-an win? His personality was criticized for being too soft or timid, but he held firm to the Pan-Blue base. While their opponents were mired in controversy, they steadily caught every ball, eventually hitting a seemingly routine but title-winning strike by relying on the Blue-Silver Turtle tower. The repercussions of this election extended far beyond Taipei; the DPP failed to win any of the five northern Keelung and Taoyuan cities, and. Tsai Ing-wen announced her resignation as party chair that very night. As for Huang Shan-shan, she officially joined the TPP the following year, and her quarter of the vote signaled that Taipei was no longer under the sole control of the Blue and Green parties. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入回顧2020年至2022年間，台灣疫情變化與關鍵防疫決策如何重塑國內政治版圖並左右首都選情。
  • 解析前衛福部長陳時中如何從聲勢頂峰的「防疫英雄」，轉變為背負施政包袱與民怨焦點的民進黨參選人。
  • 梳理2022年台北市長選戰前期的三腳督局勢，剖析蔣萬安、陳時中與黃珊珊初期的民調消長與選戰困境。

摘要

從防疫光環到民意轉折

作者回顧了2020年台灣面對COVID-19初期的情境。當時台灣創下連續253天零本土確診紀錄，每日下午兩點的疫情記者會成為全民焦點，時任衛福部長兼指揮中心指揮官的陳時中聲勢如日中天，全民掀起「順時中」風潮。在2020年4月的假想民調中，陳時中甚至以49%的支持度大幅領先國民黨立委蔣萬安，展現問鼎首都市長寶座的強大實力。

病毒變異引發的政策風暴與中央地方角力

然而，隨著病毒不斷變異，防疫神話面臨考驗。2021年Alpha變種病毒引爆諾富特飯店與機師群聚感染，在野黨強烈抨擊指揮中心放寬機組員檢疫為「3+11」的決策。隨後疫情蔓延至萬華引發全國三級警戒，官員稱萬華為「破口」更引發地方民怨。自此，中央與台北市展開激烈政治攻防，中央下午兩點召開記者會，台北市長柯文哲則於三點召開記者會分庭抗禮，雙方更圍繞在疫苗採購、國產高端疫苗與BNT疫苗爭議上針鋒相對。

共存轉型陣痛與2022首都選戰起跑

邁入2022年春季，傳染力強大的Omicron變種病毒肆虐，迫使指揮中心逐步放棄清零，轉向以減災為目標的「與病毒共存」。在政策急轉彎的過程中，伴隨快篩試劑短缺、停課與隔離標準反覆調整，以及餐飲觀光業重創，累積的民怨轉化為執政黨的沈重包袱。陳時中從昔日的抗疫領袖，逐漸成為政策代罪羔羊。此時年底地方大選戰鼓響起，對藍營而言，台北市已連續八年由非藍營執政，是絕不能再輸的關鍵戰役。

三強鼎立的初期選情與挑戰

國民黨於2022年5月正式徵召形象清新的立委蔣萬安參選。然而蔣萬安出線初期團隊步調緩慢、行程低調，被外界諷為「佛系選舉」與「躺平」，引發藍營基層焦慮。6月初公布的民調顯示，蔣萬安雖位居首位，但與因第一線防疫累積高聲量的副市長黃珊珊差距甚微，兩人落入誤差範圍；反觀陳時中則受本土疫情與防疫爭議衝擊滑落至第三名，首都市長爭奪戰正式進入緊繃的三腳督競逐。

================================================

Do you remember that summer five years ago when the COVID-19 pandemic broke out and all of Taiwan entered a Level 3 alert? "Oh, starting today, we are raising the national alert to Level 3." >> Although the Level 3 alert led to self-imposed lockdowns and empty streets everywhere, the daily number of confirmed cases did not drop significantly. >> Looking out at Nanwan Beach, there was nothing but sand; no people were there. In the blink of an eye, those days of. having to stay at home for self-isolation, wearing masks every time we went out, and scanning QR codes to report our whereabouts are already five years in the past. And this COVID-19 virus, which impacted the entire world, also impacted the election we are looking back at today. That's right, in our "Election History" video series, we have been reviewing Taipei mayoral elections since 1994. Today, we have reached the eighth episode: the 2022 Taipei mayoral election. First, let's take a time machine back to the spring of 2020. At that time, the pandemic was still in a controllable stage, and Taiwan even set a record of 253 consecutive days without any local cases. . Back then, Taiwan had a consistent peak in viewership; it wasn't the prime-time soap operas or variety shows , but the daily 2:00 PM pandemic press conference. The epidemic command center commander standing on the stage, speaking clearly and calmly, was the then-Minister of Health and Welfare, Chen Shih-chung. At that time, to cooperate with the efforts to keep local cases at zero, everyone talked about " following Chen Shih-chung," and the five officials at the command center were even dubbed the "Epidemic Prevention Dream Team." He wore a floral shirt to Kenting to promote the "New Lifestyle for Disease Prevention" campaign, and the floral shirt instantly saw a surge in inquiries, turning him into an unlikely viral marketing influencer. That April, TVBS conducted a. hypothetical poll for the Taipei mayoral race, and Chen Shih-chung took 49%, leaving KMT legislator Chiang Wan-an's 35%far behind. Suddenly, a pandemic commander became a top candidate for mayor of the capital city. All of this was built on the premise of completely blocking the entry of overseas cases. However, things soon took a sharp turn after the virus mutated. From the political bickering over whether Wanhua was the outbreak's origin, to the later chaos surrounding masks, rapid tests, and vaccines, as well as the policy contradiction between "Zero-COVID" and " living with the virus," the inconveniences people endured and the. economic impact finally erupted as collective public grievances at that moment. This battle against the pandemic went from a time when everyone was happy to "follow Chen Shih-chung" to becoming the ruling party's biggest political burden, ultimately becoming the key factor that influenced the 2022 local elections. By the way, the candidates ' academic theses have also become a major focus of public attention. Today, we will look back at the battle for the capital that followed the lifting of pandemic restrictions, discussing the fourth-generation pandemic commander and Ko Wen-je's successor. Who will be able to stand out in this race for the capital? Hello, I'm Xiao. Niu. Welcome to "Xiao Niu Talks Politics ." The story begins back in 2020 in Taiwan. During the early stages of the COVID-19 outbreak, Taiwan was consistently a global front-runner in epidemic prevention, but no matter how well we prepared, we couldn't keep up with the speed of viral mutations. By the end of 2020, the Alpha variant emerged, with a transmission rate 60% higher than the original COVID-19 virus . Just like that, the virus was quietly brought into the country, causing cluster infections. In late April, a cluster broke out at the Novotel hotel involving China Airlines pilots. Opposition parties pointed the finger at the Command Center for relaxing. quarantine rules for flight crews to "3 + 11"—three days of home quarantine followed by 11 days of self-health management. After the Novotel cluster spiraled out of control, the virus spread rapidly throughout the greater Taipei area, with Wanhua District—a densely populated area—starting to see confirmed cases of unknown origin. At the time, Deputy Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang’s remark calling Wanhua the "breakout point" infuriated the local residents. From that moment on, the greater Taipei area entered a Level 3 alert, and the central and local governments began an endless war of words. The Command Center held its usual 2 p.m. press conference, while the Taipei City Government held theirs.

at 3 p.m. Chen Shih-chung and Ko Wen-je became the main rivals in this pandemic arena, and the key point of contention was vaccines. Facing a vaccine shortage , opposition parties criticized the ruling DPP for using ideology to block imported vaccines in order to protect the domestic Medigen vaccine. For example, they slammed Chen Shih-chung for accusing the BNT vaccine of being repackaged in China during his testimony , calling it the spreading of misinformation. However, the DPP government insisted that with the whole world scrambling for vaccines and many middlemen involved, they had to stick to a government-to-government principle with original manufacturer authorization to ensure quality and avoid contract. disputes, especially regarding the BNT vaccine, which had to be shipped directly from the German factory. In the end, the pandemic had devolved into a situation where everyone was just talking past each other. Chen Shih-chung insisted that "3 + 11" was not the breakout point for the local outbreak, while Ko Wen-je threw down a harsh challenge, saying "we'll see what happens." Later, Ko scolded Chen for " not knowing what he's doing while drawing a paycheck," to which the DPP replied that emotional outbursts during the pandemic were entirely unnecessary. As the pandemic heated up, so did the rhetoric of politicians, naturally heightening anxiety among the public and making it increasingly difficult to separate pandemic prevention from. politics. By the spring of 2022, the Omicron variant struck, shifting the debate toward whether to "zero-out" or " coexist" with the virus. In early April , Chen Shih-chung admitted that a zero-COVID policy was no longer feasible . The central government set disaster reduction as the goal, effectively pivoting away from the zero-case target . However, during this policy U-turn, rapid test kits were in short supply, and quarantine and school suspension rules were constantly revised. Combined with the long-term border closures, the catering and tourism industries suffered immensely. At this point, Chen's role as commander became two-sided; to his supporters, he was the hero who led Taiwan through a once-in-a-century pandemic, but to. others, he was the face of the pandemic's toll. April 2022. The highly transmissible Omicron variant spread throughout the community. By April 30, daily confirmed cases exceeded 15,000. While transmission was rampant, the mortality rate was relatively low. The Command Center began rolling out relaxation policies, shortening home quarantine to "3 + 4" days and scrapping the SMS contact tracing system, all in hopes of accelerating a return to normal life. Meanwhile, as the pandemic began to ease , the drums of war for the year-end elections began to beat. For the "Blue" camp, Taipei had been without a Blue mayor for eight full years. In 2014, Sean Lien, and in 2018, Ting Shou-chung , both saw their vote shares stuck at around the 40%base. In 2018, the latter lost to Ko Wen-je by just over 3,000 votes. Therefore, the 2022 battle was one the KMT simply could not afford to lose. At the time, the candidate with the highest support within the party was , without question, Legislator Chiang Wan-an. With his bright, youthful appearance and credentials as a corporate lawyer, Chiang was much more marketable compared to the older generation of KMT heavyweights. He first won a legislative seat in Zhongshan and Beisongshan in 2016, and in 2020, he. successfully defended his seat and was re-elected despite the strong headwinds of the "Resist China, Protect Taiwan" movement. Of course, his family background is the most frequently mentioned topic; Chiang Wan-an's grandmother was Chang Ya-jo, and his father, Chiang Hsiao-yen, changed his surname to Chiang in 2005.
